paragraphs.heading: Two climate states
paragraphs.text: Over its long history, Earth's climate has swung between two main states, greenhouse and icehouse, each lasting millions of years. A greenhouse Earth has no continental glaciers anywhere on the planet. It also carries high levels of carbon dioxide and other greenhouse gases, and its sea surface temperatures run from 28 °C in the tropics to 0 °C in the polar regions. Earth has spent about 85% of its history in this state.

paragraphs.heading: What it is not
paragraphs.text: A greenhouse Earth is different from a runaway greenhouse effect, an irreversible tipping point like the one under way on Venus. The IPCC judges that human activity has virtually no chance of setting off such a runaway. It is also distinct from the "Hothouse Earth" of the most extreme projections of modern climate change. Likewise, an icehouse is not the same as a glacial period: glacials and interglacials are shorter phases, usually under a million years, that alternate inside an icehouse.

paragraphs.heading: What drives the swings
paragraphs.text: The main suspected drivers are greenhouse gases, chiefly carbon dioxide (CO₂) and to a lesser degree methane (CH₄), along with changes in Earth's orbit, slow changes in the solar constant, and shifts in oceans and mountain building caused by moving tectonic plates. Rock records show that greenhouse states go together strongly with high CO₂. Higher amounts of these gases trap the Sun's energy in the atmosphere. Active volcanoes release huge amounts of CO₂ and methane, enough to cause a greenhouse effect. High CO₂ was long read as a feedback rather than an independent cause, though causes in the rocks themselves that push CO₂ and climate have been found.

paragraphs.heading: Today's icehouse
paragraphs.text: Earth today is in an icehouse state, with ice sheets at both poles at once. In this state greenhouse gas levels and global temperatures tend to be lower, and the planet swings between glacial and interglacial periods as ice sheets grow and shrink dramatically. The present icehouse, the Quaternary Ice Age, began about 2.58 million years ago, though an Antarctic ice sheet has existed for about 34 million years. The current mild interglacial began around 11,800 years ago.

paragraphs.heading: How oceans helped cool Earth
paragraphs.text: Moving plates and the opening or closing of ocean gateways seem to play a crucial part in pushing Earth into an icehouse. Such shifts can carry cool deep water up to the surface, helping ice sheets grow at the poles. The Tasmanian Gateway opened 36.5 million years ago between Australia and Antarctica, and the Drake Passage opened 32.8 million years ago between South America and Antarctica. Both are thought to have let the Antarctic ice sheet form. The closing of the Isthmus of Panama and the Indonesian seaway about 3 to 4 million years ago may also have played a part.

paragraphs.heading: Glacial cycles and the future
paragraphs.text: Inside an icehouse, only about 20% of the time is spent in warmer interglacials. The swings between glacials and interglacials come mainly from variations in Earth's movement around the Sun, the Milankovitch cycles: the tilt of the axis, the shape of the orbit and the wobble of Earth's spin. Model simulations suggest that, because of CO₂ emissions, the present interglacial will last at least another 100,000 years, with the Northern Hemisphere losing its ice completely. Once the Quaternary Ice Age ends, Earth is expected to return to a greenhouse state.
